From the New York Commercial Advertiser, June 1 1 , 1842 The Earthquake þÿ Eveiy arrival from the West Indies brings some new particulars of the ravages and disasters attendant on the great convulsion of the 7th of May ; and the first accounts, instead of being exaggerated t appear to have understated the destruction of life and property There is however, one exception to this remark. The calamities at Gonaives, as reported by Captain Varina, of the brig Pandora, arrived this week at Boston, were happily confined to ilie ruin of houses ; the inhabitants had timely warning in a groaning sound; which they readily understood, and rushing into the streets, all escaped with life but two. Most of the buildings in the place were destroyed. A letter Irom Cape Haytien, received in Philadelphia, estimates the loss ol life at between eight and nine thousand. A friend of the writer succeeded in saving his wile and one þÿchild but his two oiher children -perished in the ruins of Ins dwelling. The horrors of pillage were added to those of the earth quake. The writer says : þÿ The hour being that in which the inhabitants were preparing tor their evening meal, the falling in of the roofs and rafters scattered I he fires, which seized upon them, and in an incredibly snort space of time the whole woodwork of the city was in llames ; by 8 o clock the country people poured into the city, armed with machetes, knives and gnus, and commenced the work of pillage and minder, killing every one who offered any resistance to their depredations. þÿ The houses and stores

of the few whites and principal merchants were the first to be attacked. These were soon sacked, and every thing in the shape of movable property that, was not covered up in the ruins was taken possession of. Bands of eight or ten of the plundereis would meet in the streets and contend for the spoils, fiequently leaving on the ground half of tht-tr number dead or desperately wounded. Such a scene, as 1 am informed by eve witnesses, was scarcely ever beheld. Beneath the ruins trie cues of the wound'. .1 and dying, for succor, were heard in vain, and in many cases four da\s elapsed before hi v efforts were made for their extrication. þÿ To day one person was brought out alive wl.o had i, red fifteen days under a lieu of wall. Every merchant that could escape made fi r the shipping, where upward of one hundred were crowded in lour vessels. The sin vi vois sleep in the country, in the fields, none daring to trust themselves as yet under any cover The stench from corrupted bodies was such that at one time it wi s feared some pestilence would break out j I t the fire and the lime stone (which the heat has converted into quick lime) is daily purj. fvint: the air. SUSPECTED ATTACK UPON HER MAJESTY. Yesterday afternoon a feeling ol most intense and painful excitement was occasioned throughout trie metropolis, by the circulation of a report that another treasonable allempt had been that day made upon the life ol the Queen, as her Majesty was proceeding from Buckingham Palace to the Chapel Royal, St. James's, to attend Divine Service, in accordance with her usual custom. From the inquiries we have made, and from what has been permitted to transpire, the following authentic particulars ol an alleged attempt to shoot at the Queen may be iclied on. The fact of such an attempt being made, must, ii would appear, have been unobserved by her Majesty or any of her attendants, the royal cortege proceeding uninterruptedly on its course; and the matter would probably have passed off unnoticed, had not the act been witnessed by a young man, about 18 years of age, who observed the person pull the trigger ol the pistol and distinctly heard the snap, although he saw no Hash He instantly seized him, as well as if le instrument he had in his hand, arid seeing no

AT3So policeman near, dragged him in the direction I tie royal carriages had gone, until he met Police constable Heart), A 56, who had been doing duty at the gardengate leading to the Chapel Royal, through which her Majesty had just entered, to whom he said, 1 have taken this young man and brought him to you, because I saw him present a pistol at her Majesty ;" and at the same time he showed the policeman the pistol he had in his hand. The constatile (who. it must be observed, has been but three months in the force), however, instead of immediately taking the accused in custody, laughed, believing the charge to be a hoax, and walked on. Close behind him was another policeman, named Ulaxton, A 134. to whom the young man also spoke, hut lie treated him m the same manner, and saying " Pooh, pooh, it's all nonsense," likewise walked on. The young man, therefore, finding that the officers of the law had refused to lake charge of the accused, allowed him to depart, retaining, however, possession of the pistol. At that juncture another police constable. Partridge, A 136, an experienced officer, came up, and seeing the pistol in his hand, said to him, ' What are you doing with that pistol;" The young man told him that he had taken it from a youth who had attempted to shoot the Queen, and w hom he had just let go. the two policemen to whom he had taken him having refused to take him into custody. Partridge immediately told his Informant that he must accompany him, in order that a pro-
per inquiry might be made into the matter, to the station house, in Gardiner's lane, Westminster, whither they instantly proceeded, followed by a crowd of nearly 3000 persons.

Amidst the terrible and fatal series of cala mities which have stricked the Royal House of France, none have tallert more suddenly on that devoted family, none have flung a deeper gloom over the future destinies of that country, than the accident which has cost the life of Ferdinand of Orleans, the lieu apparent to the throne. How irregular, how mysterious, how severe are those dispensations of Providence, which appear to leave within the reach of common chance lives which have been so oiten and so wonderfully preserved from the designs ol conspirators, and the menaces of anarchy ! The dagger ol Louvois proved lalai to the elder branch of the Bourbons, in spite ot the infant scion which sprang from the Duke de Beiuu's grave ; and it is impossible to view without the deepest anxiety the recurtence of a state of things so pregnant with danger to the French monarchy and to the institutions of that country. An aged Kino and an infant heir seem to belong lo the most trying periods of French history þÿ indeed infinitely less trying than periods thai which awaits the country now, lor even amidst the Uistui bances and the excesses of homer regencies, the person of the Sovereign was sacied, and the traditional principles ol the Royal authority were inviolate. At the present time it is needless to enlarge on the importance of the highest personal qualities, the resolution of manhood, the experience of life, and the authority ot a mature reason, m the ruler of France. The history of the last

twelve years, and the character of the present Kino, sutiiciently prove that no weaker Prince could have surmounted the frightful difficulties of his position. The Kino will, on this occasion, meet w ith the warmest and truest expression ot the confidence and regard enteitained in Fiance and throughout Europe for his family, and lor the institutions which he has consolidated, þÿ The depth and the extent of the sympathy which this occurrence will call forth must prove how deep and how extensive. is the reliance of Europe on the maintenance of the present reigning family ; and it must strengthen the general feeling that the dungeis and chances which have alieady marked in such frightful characters the history of the House of Bourbon, have rendered the lives of the survivors of that race more essential to the peace of the world and to the prosperity of Prance. W hichever way we turn our thoughts, some fresh coincidence suggests itself to the mind, some fresh manifestation of extraordinary and incomprehensible power appears to i ise out of every vicissitude in the fate of these august and unfortunate families. Of the three young men, almost contemporaries in age; who were born heirs to that throne, or raised to that condition, and who, in the ordinary course of human life, seemed destined at least to live through the greater part of this century, and to play no obscure or ordinary part in the course of human affairs, the sole survivor is the exiled heir of the elder branch. The

Duke de Keichstadt dies at Vienna, stripped of the royal ornaments thrown by fortune on his cradle. The Duke de Bordeaux leads the objectless and uncertain existence of a pretender. The Duke d'Orleans suddenly perishes in the streets of Paris at the very moment when his file seemed of most importance to his familv and lug cmntrv

- ATIS It is of course premature to speculate on the arrangements which may he hereafter contemplated hv the French Governm nt. þÿ We alluded the other day to the peculiar gravity and importance ol the duties which probably await the newly-elected Chamber of Deputies, but assuredly no man fort-saw that a Regency Bill would be the first act to be submitted to that body. The Royal family is happily not wanting in members of an age and character to support the dynasty ; but the Heir Apparent is an :nfant, and in all human probability the supreme power inust pass into the hands of a Regent upon the demise of the present Kino. '1 he Duke de Nemours is obviously the Prince whose position, as eldest uncle of the Heir Apparent, points him out as the fittest person lo act, in case of a minority, although the unbroken health and unabated vigour of the Ktr.c load us to hope that the present reign may yet he prolonged for many years. But, under all the circumstances which may arise out of this distressing and unexpected ctisis, there is noone personage to whom France will look with more hope and trust than to the widowed Duchess of Orleans. That Princess, more illustrious for her virtues and tier character than for her birth and station, has won, to a retnarkabie degree, the confidence ot Eouts Philippe, and the respect of the nation. As the mother of the infant heir, she cannot but exercise a most important influence over his futuie destinies ; and to whomsoever the Legislature may confide t fie politi-

cal power of the guardian of that Prince, she naturally ca'ied. as the surviving parent of the future King of the French, to duties of no common magnitude. Even amidst the gloom and grief of her affliction she appears to be marked out by this portentous event to maintain tfie rights of her son. and lo prepare a Sovereign for his people ; and if we are not mistaken, she is eminently qualified to discharge the high, though melancholy, duties which may devolve upon her.
